judged_text: The util unconditionally injects the literal string "refresh_token" as data.refresh_token whenever the parsed response lacks one — which is every response in sharing mode, since the sync endpoint returns only access token and expiry — and callers persist that value to the credential table. Every synced app's stored credential carries a fake refresh token; any downstream missing-refresh_token guard (e.g. zoom's) now passes on garbage, and if sharing is later disabled the direct-refresh path sends refresh_token="refresh_token" and the integration fails permanently until re-auth.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the util mutates the parsed data by setting `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` whenever the parsed response lacks a refresh token. In sharing mode (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`), the code intentionally parses with `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (which does not require `refresh_token`), so this branch will trigger for sync-endpoint responses that omit refresh tokens. This can overwrite and persist a fake refresh token: e.g. in `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) }` will overwrite the existing real `refresh_token` with the injected literal string, and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: o365AuthCredentials } })` persists it to the DB. That matches the finding’s core concern about corrupting stored credentials with a dummy refresh token.
